name: C++

facts.ai_role: The performance layer underneath the Python surface: PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp, and most inference runtimes are C++.
facts.steward: ISO/IEC JTC1 SC22 WG21 standards committee

title: C++ in AI: The Performance Layer Beneath Python
answer: C++ is a compiled, general purpose programming language first released in 1985 and standardized by ISO/IEC JTC1 SC22 WG21. In AI work it is the performance layer beneath the Python surface: PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp and most inference runtimes are C++. A reader deciding whether to use it should know that it buys direct control of speed and memory at the cost of a steeper learning curve than Python, and that the official site is a standards and community hub rather than a tutorial.

sections.body: C++ is a compiled programming language whose first release dates to 1985, and it is stewarded by the ISO/IEC JTC1 SC22 WG21 standards committee rather than by a single company. The official site, isocpp.org, is the public face of that committee and of the wider community around it. In the AI stack it occupies the performance layer underneath the Python surface: PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp and most inference runtimes are written in C++. The site's own material reflects this positioning indirectly, through standardization work on machine learning in SG19 and on low latency, games, embedded and financial trading in SG14, groups whose concerns overlap heavily with AI systems work. It is not a framework and not a model library, it is the language in which the fast parts of those things are built.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The concrete AI jobs C++ does are the ones where space and time constraints are real: training and inference engine internals, custom CUDA kernels, model serving runtimes, edge and embedded deployment, and the data path of high throughput pipelines. The site's CppCon 2026 keynote description frames this in terms of industry data from SlashData and IDC documenting sustained demand for programmers who can operate under real space and time constraints, and it points to standard library performance enhancers such as std::simd and std::execution as current work. Where C++ is the best choice is where Python is too slow, too memory hungry or too unpredictable, and where a runtime must be shipped as a native binary. The site does not rank languages or claim C++ is best for experimentation, and nothing in the pages read supports a claim that it is the right first language for model research.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: C++ has a reputation for a steep learning curve, and the official material does not contradict that, though it also does not present a beginner curriculum. The site is a standards and community hub: blog posts, standards paper mailings, meeting minutes, survey announcements and conference promotion. A newcomer will find the annual global C++ developer survey described as a one pager taking about ten minutes, trip reports from ISO meetings, and pointers to CppCon, but not a structured tutorial path. Prerequisites implied by the content are systems knowledge such as memory, compilation and linking, and enough mathematics to follow machine learning work in SG19. The site notes that it is now more than 45 years since C++ was first conceived, so the language carries a large surface area and a long history that a learner has to navigate.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem around C++ is visible on the site through the standardization process itself. Regular mailings of new standards papers appear, along with minutes from SG14 on low latency, games, embedded and financial trading, and SG19 on machine learning. Compiler vendors are active participants: GCC 16.1 is reported with C++26 reflection, contracts, safety hardening and C++20 enabled by default, with C++20 modules support still experimental behind -fmodules. Conferences and talks are promoted, including CppCon 2026 in Aurora, Colorado, starting September 12, and a CppCon 2025 talk on JSON serialization performance. The annual developer survey results, including write-in responses, are shared with committee participants and tool vendors to inform evolution and tooling, which is an unusually direct feedback loop between users and the language's direction.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: C++ is built for speed and memory control in production rather than for quick experiments, and the site's content is consistent with that emphasis. The C++26 work highlighted includes reflection, an initial round of memory safety hardening, and standard library performance enhancers such as std::simd and std::execution. The C++29 working draft is reported to include a new annex cataloging every case of core language undefined behavior, described as a first step toward addressing it systematically, plus draft profiles for stronger portable memory safety guarantees now being prototyped. The cost of this control is that the programmer manages more detail than in a managed language, and the site does not claim that C++ is a fast path for throwaway scripts or notebook style exploration.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The site supports the view that C++ is a current standard rather than a legacy choice. The ISO committee completed technical work on C++26 in March 2026 and in June voted the first additions into the working draft for C++29, and compiler support is shipping, with GCC 16.1 enabling C++20 by default. The CppCon 2026 keynote description cites SlashData and IDC data on sustained growth in demand for professional programmers, especially those who know languages that can operate under real space and time constraints. For someone choosing it for work, that points to roles in inference runtimes, serving infrastructure, kernels and edge deployment. The site does not publish salary figures, job counts or adoption percentages, so any specific career claim beyond this would go beyond what the material settles.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: The polyglot pattern the site implies is C++ underneath and something else on top. Python is the surface where models are described and experiments run, while C++ supplies libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp and most inference runtimes. The site's own example of AI in practice is a blog post by Giovanni Dicanio about double checking AI generated output, in which Claude reviewed the WinReg C++ library and reported zero length bugs in the string getters of the RegKey class, noting that the binary returning getters were correctly guarded against a zero data size while the string getters were not. That is a small illustration of the division of labor: AI tools assist around the edges, while the C++ code itself still has to be read and verified by a person.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: C++ is weak where rapid iteration matters more than control, and the site does not pretend otherwise. Memory safety is the most visible open area: the C++29 working draft adds an annex cataloging all core language undefined behavior, draft profiles for portable memory safety guarantees are still being prototyped, and the committee's next six months include a telecon line by line review of a proposal to systematically address undefined behavior, both aimed at C++29. Modules support in GCC 16.1 is still experimental and must be enabled with -fmodules. The official material does not say how quickly profiles will be usable in production compilers, does not compare C++ against other languages on safety or speed, and does not offer a beginner curriculum, so a reader should treat those as unsettled rather than decided.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
